title: The services page a recruiting firm actually needs
metaTitle: The services page a recruiting firm needs
excerpt: Each search offer needs an outcome, a boundary, and a way to brief it. A grid of vague capabilities does not help a hiring manager who has been burned.
alt: Clothes on wooden hangers suspended from a white branch against a plain wall, a sparse display standing in for offers that should be few and distinct.
caption: A few pieces, clearly hung, are easier to choose than a crowded rail. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should each block on a recruiting services page contain?
faqs.answer: Write an outcome, a boundary, and a next step. The outcome is what the hiring manager holds at the end, such as a capped shortlist against a scorecard. The boundary is the work you will not do. The next step is a brief for that specific search, not a general contact link.

faqs.question: How many services should a recruiting firm list?
faqs.answer: Most firms should show three to five searches they actually want to be hired for. One honest offer is stronger than eight tiles. Remove paused work. Group two roles only when the brief, the fee shape, and the refusal are the same.

faqs.question: Why does a capability grid fail a hiring manager?
faqs.answer: Icons for sourcing, assessment, and advisory describe activities with no edge, and they describe almost every firm. Visitors have time to read only about a quarter of the words on a typical visit, so they will not infer your offer from a grid. Headings that name the search let them choose.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A recruiting firm services page should list the work in the hiring manager's language. Each offer needs an outcome, a boundary, and a next step, which is to brief the search. A grid of vague capabilities does not help a buyer who has been burned before. Google's people-first guidance asks whether someone leaves a page knowing enough to take the next step. "Talent solutions" does not answer that. A named search does.

Write one block per offer you actually want to be hired for. If you cannot say what is finished, what you will not do, and how the brief starts, it is not an offer yet. It is a heading.

## Outcome, boundary, and the brief

Treat every service as three sentences, in that order.

The outcome is the state the hiring manager is buying. A shortlist of operators who have run a single plant, scored against a written scorecard. A confidential replacement of a sales lead, with the incumbent still in the seat until the offer. Not "access to talent."

The boundary is where the work stops. You do not run the onboarding. You do not fill the two coordinator seats that appear in the same budget meeting. You do not start outreach before the scorecard is signed. A burned buyer is looking for the edge, because the last firm expanded the work until the original role was a footnote.

The next step is the brief. The link in the block should say "Brief this search," and it should carry the offer's name into the form. A single "contact" link at the bottom of twelve tiles throws the buyer back into a general inbox. They have already told you which search they want by choosing the block.

If a block cannot hold those three sentences, cut the offer from the page until it can. A shorter list of real searches beats a complete-looking menu.

## Use the words they use on the requisition

Internal names are a common failure. The firm says "embedded partnership," "talent advisory," and "executive mandate." The hiring manager says "we need a plant manager" or "we need to replace our head of sales without announcing it." The page should use the second set.

Read the last ten intake notes. Circle the nouns the client used in the first five minutes. Those nouns are the labels. If your best work is a retained search for a first-time finance lead in a founder-owned company, the heading should say that. The method can sit in the boundary sentence. The method should not be the heading.

A short list of swaps:

- "Retained leadership search" can stay if the next line names the roles.
- "Contingent staffing" should say which seats, and that you are paid only if they hire, if that is true.
- "Market mapping" should say it is a map, not a shortlist, so nobody briefs it expecting candidates.
- "Interview training" should say who is trained, the hiring panel or your researchers, and that it is not a search.

Do not add a glossary that translates your brand words back into plain words. Use the plain words as the headings. The brand can live in how the sentences sound, not in a private vocabulary the buyer has to learn before they can brief you.

## How many offers belong on the page

Most firms should show three to five searches. More than that and the page becomes a directory of everything the team has ever tried. Fewer than that is fine if it is honest. One offer, written with a clear boundary, is a stronger page than eight tiles.

Group only when the buyer would group them. "Plant leadership" can hold a plant manager and a maintenance lead if the brief, the fee shape, and the refusal are the same. Do not group "finance" and "sales" because both sit in a C-suite diagram. The burned buyer is not shopping a diagram. They have one seat open.

Give each offer the same structure so the eye can compare. Heading. Outcome. Boundary. One proof line if you have a true one. The brief link. Resist a unique layout for the offer a partner is most proud of. Pride is not a reading order.

If an offer is paused, remove it. A services page is a promise of current work. Leaving a paused offer up because the design looks empty is how you collect briefs you will decline. Decline them in the boundary of a live offer instead.

## What a capability grid wastes

A grid of icons fails this buyer in a specific way. Each cell is a noun with no edge. Sourcing. Assessment. Diversity. Onboarding. Advisory. The cells are true of almost every firm that disappointed them. The grid also spends the page on activities instead of decisions. Sourcing is not an outcome. A shortlist with a cap is an outcome.

The grid is comforting in a workshop because it looks complete. Completeness is the wrong goal. Nielsen Norman Group's page research is blunt about attention: on the visits people do make, they have time to read only about a quarter of the words, and the average visit lasts a little less than a minute. A grid asks them to infer your offer from twelve icons in that minute. They will not. They will leave with the same category they arrived with.

Replace the grid with the three-sentence blocks. If you need a scan, use the headings as the scan. A person who reads only the headings should be able to say which search is theirs. If the headings are "Discover, Engage, Deliver," they cannot.

Keep one sentence somewhere on the page for what you refuse across all offers. No resume spray. No search without a scorecard. No second role slipped into the same fee. That sentence does more than a row of capabilities, because it is a decision.

## Confidential work still needs a public sentence

Some of the best searches cannot be described with a client name. That is not a reason to retreat into vague headings. Describe the constraint without the company. A replacement for a head of sales while the person is still in the seat. The brief stays with two people on the client side. You do not post the role. A hiring manager who has lived that situation will recognize it. A stranger looking for a name will not find one.

Say what you will not put on the site even after the search closes. If you never name clients, say that near the offers, so the absence of logos looks like a rule rather than an empty portfolio. Point the proof at decisions. The services page can hold one unnamed constraint per offer. The longer story belongs on a proof page, where there is room for what you decided and what you refused.

Separate candidate-facing language from these blocks. A page written for hiring managers should not invite "passive talent" inside the same tile. If you need a candidate door, give it one line at the end of the page: where a person may send a background, and that sending it is not briefing a search. Mixing the two audiences is how a burned buyer decides you are a job board with a professional fee.

## Order the page the way a brief happens

Open with the offer you most want a burned hiring manager to recognize. Not the offer with the largest fee. Not the offer that is easiest to staff. The one that matches the role sentence on the homepage. If the homepage says plant leadership, the first block on this page should be that search, written out, not a teaser back to the homepage.

Then the offers that are easy to confuse with it. A confidential replacement next to a public search, so the boundary between them is visible. A mapping project next to a retained search, so nobody pays mapping rates and expects a shortlist.

End the page with the brief, repeated, and a line on what to have ready. The role title. Why the seat is open. What the last attempt got wrong. You do not need their whole org chart to say whether you should talk.

Do not bury fees inside every block if the pricing page already holds the shape. One line is enough: this search is retained, in the shape you have already published. Do not send them away before the boundary is clear. The services page has to stand on its own for the visitor who never sees the homepage.

## A block you can draft this week

Sit with one live search and write the block in a document, not in the design tool.

Heading: the role family and the company shape.
Outcome: what they hold at the end, with a count if you use one.
Boundary: two things you will not do.
Proof: one constraint from a real search, with the client unnamed if you must. A family-owned mill needed a plant manager who had run a night shift, and the firm refused to widen the scorecard to "any operations leader."
Action: brief this search.

Read it to the person who runs that work. If they say the firm also does many other things, do not add those things to the block. Put them in another block or leave them off the site. The block is a door, not a biography of the practice.

When the blocks are true, the page stops being a menu of capabilities and becomes a way to start the right search. The about page can then do a different job. Read [who should be named behind the search](/blog/how-a-recruiting-firm-should-write-an-about-page) once the offers are specific enough that a stranger would care who runs them.

If you want help turning a list of capabilities into offers with edges, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The work is the sentences first, then the page that holds them.
